toc.title: Pathway four: feeling your stuck defensive state

blocks.p: You're probably doing a ton of trauma recovery and general wellness kinds of things, and it can get overwhelming. So I want to share [four buckets](piece:snb242-four-wellness-pathways), or pathways, that you can place all of your efforts into. I want to help you sort your efforts, see what they're doing, and maybe see where you need to grow.

This comes up consistently and predictably in my client work. What is your goal, and how are you going about it? Your goal is probably to get unstuck, to reduce anxiety or depression or anger or rage or overwhelm, or fill in the blank. Maybe all of them. But what avenues are you taking to reach that goal?
Here are the four pathways:

ol: The basics: the foundational things that have to be in place.
Coping: reducing defensive activation in the moment.
Practicing safety: building up your safety state.
Feeling your stuck defensive state: directly feeling and relieving the flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze you're stuck in.

blocks.p: The first one is baseline stuff, the things you should have in place. If you don't have them in place, all your other efforts probably won't be as helpful as they could be.

That's foundational things like eating healthy enough, drinking enough water, and getting enough sleep. We don't need perfection. I don't need you to be hyper nutritional, measuring your water every day, wearing a backpack full of water to make sure you get a ton.

Just enough. Good enough. I can't tell you what number that is. But if you're living off candy, that's probably not good enough. If you're living off fats and sugars, soda, pizza, that's probably not good enough. So make improvements in that area. It's unbelievably important to the other three pathways.

Sleep is huge. I have sleep apnea, and if I don't get good enough sleep, I feel it the rest of the day. Everything becomes so much more difficult. So sleep enough, eat well enough, drink enough water, get enough movement, be healthy enough.

Pathway two is where I think people get stuck a lot, and it's typically where they are when they start coming into therapy. You probably have some anxiety or anger or depression, fill in the blank, and you're trying to figure out how to cope with it. How do I make it go away, or how do I reduce it?

I don't blame you at all. Of course you want it to reduce, if not go away. But what you're doing is decreasing defensive activation through hacks you're finding online, like jumping into freezing cold water, taking cold showers, or putting a bag of frozen peas on your chest to reduce anxiety. Those things might help you reduce anxiety, and I'm happy about that.

But they're very temporary. They do not resolve the problem. And what they may actually do is trigger your dorsal vagal state and numb you out. In essence, it puts you into a little bit of shutdown. So yes, your anxiety is gone. But are you more connected to the present moment? Do you love yourself more now? It just kind of helps the feelings go away for a while.

One of my clients was told by a psychiatrist to squeeze his thumbnail when he's feeling anxious. To me, it's just a hack. Maybe it does something for you. But if it does, does it help you love yourself more? Does it connect you with your loved ones more? Do you feel less guilt in your life? Do you feel less perpetual anxiety? Probably not. Maybe in that moment, because now you're causing yourself pain or distracting yourself, and there's value to that.

So what are you doing that fits into this bucket? Things like counting backwards when you're anxious, or playing with a fidget when you're anxious or angry or depressed. Those are coping. You're trying to reduce defensive activation, and that totally has a place. If you need to numb yourself out because you're feeling suicidal, go ahead, watch TV until you feel less suicidal and can do something about it. (Numb is better than not alive.) I don't think there's anything wrong with that at all.

So coping definitely has a place, but it is not the answer. If you're going into therapy seeking more coping, that's fine, but hopefully your therapist can do more for you and get you to the next two pathways.
Pathway three is practicing safety. This is what we therapists honestly miss, and it's probably what you're missing in your efforts.

How do you feel safe? What triggers feelings of comfort for you? What helps bring you to the present moment? What helps you breathe easier? What helps you feel appreciation, maybe gratitude, love? Maybe not happiness, or maybe happiness. Maybe just contentment, or awe. Some of these might be easier to reach than others.
What helps you feel safe and connected to yourself, to the environment, or to others?

ul: Connection to yourself means having enough self-compassion to look inward and be open to all of your experiences, even the uncomfortable ones.

Connection to the environment comes through your senses. Do you know which sensory triggers bring you to your safety state? What tastes, smells, or textures help you just be and breathe, and that's enough?

blocks.p: I'm not saying it's easy. But I think it's extremely important. If you can practice feeling safe and literally build up the strength of your biological ventral vagal safety pathways, you just won't need coping as much. It'll probably still pop up, sure. But your distress tolerance goes up. Your feelings of connection to yourself, others, and the environment go up. Your ability to be mindful of your experience, positive and negative, goes up.

And the defensive activation you're stuck in, flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze, eases up too. It doesn't exactly solve the problem. But it makes life way more manageable without relying on coping skills or hacks, and it really reduces the intensity and frequency of your defensive activation.

Nobody thinks or talks this way, honestly. Even in therapy, we focus on what the problem is and how to make it go away. Well, part of making the problem go away is practicing feeling safe. As we do that, things get better little by little by little. It's not a hack. It's a long process.
Irene Lyon made a similar point about practice when she was on the podcast:

q: Even doing one-on-one work every week for a year, from what I've seen is not enough. You have to be practicing when you're not there.

blocks.h: Pathway four: feeling your stuck defensive state

blocks.p: Pathway four is directly feeling and relieving your stuck defensive state, whether it's flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze. It depends hugely on pathways one and three: the basics, and feeling safe, grounded, and connected to yourself in the present moment, even when uncomfortable things come up.

Say it's momentary anxiety. Rather than coping it away through some hack, you say, "Okay, I'm feeling anxious." Not "Why am I feeling this way?" but "Let me feel this way. I can handle this. I can permit myself to feel anxious, or angry, or irritated, or depressed and numb." You have enough safety activation because you've put in the daily work to practice being safe. Now you have such a strong foundation of safety that you can allow yourself to feel defensive activation.
And you can use pathway four for more than the momentary anxiety spike. You can intentionally feel the stuck flight activation that the momentary anxiety comes from.

Pathway four is hugely important for truly recovering from a stuck defensive state, for relieving trauma. You can practice safety every day and build up the strength of your safety pathways, and a lot of good can come from that. But that next step of getting unstuck, finding more emotional freedom and deeper connection with yourself, has to come through pathway four. And that relies entirely on your ability to stay grounded in the present moment, in your safety state, and then to:

ol: Validate your experiences, even the difficult ones.
Feel them, lightly at first, and over time even deeply: the stuck defensive activation, and the memories, images, and textures that come along with it.

blocks.p: You can do this in doses, and it's a really good idea. We don't want to go all the way into defensive activation all at once. Little doses here and there are probably best.

I liken it, especially with freeze activation, to skipping stones. You throw a stone across the water, and it just touches the water before coming back up. That's a good metaphor for how to handle defensive activation as you start down pathway four: lightly touch upon defense, come back to safety. Lightly touch upon defense, come back to safety.
That's called pendulation. You can do it on purpose, back and forth, and as an introduction to pathway four, it's a really good idea.
If you're coping day in, day out, good for you. Do what you have to do. But can you find moments to include a tad more safety in your life? I think you can.

I had a session recently where the person said, "I have no time for any mindfulness. I have no time for practicing safety. I have no time for this, that, or the other thing." So I said, "Okay, let's take inventory of your daily life. Let's audit it. What do you do when you wake up?" And he said, "Well, usually I spend about five hours on YouTube and social media." There's five hours right there we can work with.

Many people will default to "I just have to cope. I have to get through this, because I don't have time." There's probably time. There's probably a moment. And these things can be practiced in micro moments, which have a ton of benefit to them.

ul: When you wake up, would a walk outside feel safer than lying in bed scrolling for five hours? Probably.
In the morning, can you connect with a loved one and give them a hug, or your pet? That's a moment of safety.
Can you mindfully experience how your cereal makes you feel when you eat it, the smell of your coffee, the taste of your tea?

blocks.p: These are tiny moments where you can practice safety. And while you keep coping, can you also drink more water instead of soda? Can you eat something fresh and not from fast food? Probably.

If you can do all that, be a little healthier, maybe a lot healthier, cope your way through when you need to, and feel safety in micro moments, then eventually you might be able to ask: what else do I feel? What's it really like to be me, stuck in whatever state I'm in?

You might not be close to that right now, and that's okay. Down the line, that's a question you could ask yourself. It's pretty normal in my client work. We build up so much safety that my clients get to a point where they say, "I'm ready to feel just what it's like to be me, completely. What else is within me?" And they're open to it.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: Look at all the things you're doing, and put each one into one of the four pathways.

ul: If you squeeze your thumb to feel better, which bucket does that belong in?
If you cook a fresh meal tonight, which bucket does that belong in?
If you hug your mom and tell her you love her, which bucket does that belong in?
If you meditate and feel what it's like to be you, completely, which bucket would that be in?

blocks.p: Then notice where you are, where you'd like to get to, and what you might bolster if it needs bolstering.
